section-4: Educational Technology in detail. The term combines 'education' and 'technology' (from the Greek 'techne', meaning art or skill). It is not only the use of machines; it is a systematic approach to designing, carrying out and evaluating teaching and learning using knowledge from psychology, communication, management and engineering. Its scope includes formulating objectives, analysing learner characteristics, selecting content and media, developing teaching strategies and evaluating outcomes.

Need and importance in detail. Educational technology helps teachers handle large classes, individual differences and the knowledge explosion; it makes learning interesting, concrete and self-paced; it supports distance and online education (SWAYAM, DIKSHA); and it improves the quality and efficiency of the teaching-learning process.

Types in detail. Teaching technology deals with the teaching process (planning, organising, leading and controlling teaching); instructional technology deals with the design of instruction and materials (programmed learning, modules); behavioural technology deals with modifying teacher and learner behaviour (micro-teaching, interaction analysis); and instructional design deals with systematic planning of instruction.

Approaches in detail. The hardware approach (ET-I) uses machines such as projectors, computers, radio and television, based on the physical sciences. The software approach (ET-II) uses principles of psychology to develop learning materials such as programmed instruction and teaching strategies. The systems approach combines both into an integrated system with inputs, process and outputs.
section-5: Communication in detail. The word comes from the Latin 'communis', meaning 'common'. Its elements are sender (teacher), message (content), channel or medium (speech, chalkboard, video), receiver (student), feedback and the environment. Shannon and Weaver's model and Berlo's SMCR model (Source, Message, Channel, Receiver) explain the process. Classroom communication should be two-way.

Verbal and non-verbal communication in detail. Verbal communication includes oral (lectures, discussions) and written (notes, textbooks, chalkboard) forms. Non-verbal communication includes facial expressions, eye contact, gestures, body posture, tone of voice, proximity and silence. Teachers' non-verbal cues strongly affect students' attention and feelings.

Factors affecting communication in detail. Characteristics of the sender (knowledge, clarity, attitude), the message (organisation, difficulty), the channel (suitability of media), the receiver (attention, readiness, background) and the environment (seating, lighting, noise). Feedback helps the teacher check understanding.

Barriers in detail. Physical barriers (noise, poor acoustics, distance), psychological barriers (fear, anxiety, lack of interest, prejudice), semantic barriers (difficult words, jargon, language differences), cultural barriers and organisational barriers. They can be reduced by clear language, teaching aids, a friendly climate and regular feedback.
section-6: Bloom's taxonomy in detail. Benjamin Bloom and his associates (1956) classified objectives into three domains. The cognitive domain has six levels: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis and evaluation (revised in 2001 as remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate and create). The affective domain (Krathwohl, 1964) includes receiving, responding, valuing, organisation and characterisation. The psychomotor domain (Simpson, Dave) deals with physical skills from imitation to naturalisation.

Programmed learning in detail. Based on Skinner's operant conditioning, it presents material in small steps (frames), requires active response, gives immediate feedback (knowledge of results) and allows self-pacing. Linear programming (Skinner) has all learners follow the same sequence; branching programming (Norman Crowder) sends learners to remedial frames according to their answers; mathetics (Gilbert) works backward from the final step.

Instructional system designing in detail. ISD is a systematic process of planning instruction, commonly following the ADDIE model: Analysis (needs, learners, tasks), Design (objectives, strategies, assessment), Development (materials), Implementation and Evaluation (formative and summative). It ensures that instruction is purposeful and effective.

Flanders's interaction analysis in detail. Ned Flanders (1960s) developed the Flanders Interaction Analysis Category System (FIACS) with 10 categories: teacher talk - indirect influence (1 accepts feelings, 2 praises, 3 accepts ideas, 4 asks questions) and direct influence (5 lectures, 6 gives directions, 7 criticises); student talk (8 response, 9 initiation); and 10 silence or confusion. Observers record every 3 seconds and analyse a matrix to improve teacher behaviour.
section-7: PSI in detail. The Personalized System of Instruction, or Keller Plan, was developed by Fred S. Keller in 1968. Its features are self-pacing, mastery requirement (students must master a unit before moving on), use of student proctors for testing and tutoring, emphasis on written material, and lectures used mainly for motivation. It promotes mastery learning and individual responsibility.

CAI in detail. Computer Assisted Instruction uses computers for drill and practice, tutorials, simulations, educational games and problem-solving. It gives immediate feedback, individualised pace, multimedia presentation and record keeping. Limitations include cost, need for technical skills and reduced human interaction. Examples include educational software, e-learning platforms and virtual labs.

Informatics in detail. Informatics deals with the collection, storage, processing and communication of information using computers and networks. In education it includes the use of databases, internet resources, learning management systems, digital libraries and educational management information systems (UDISE+). Advantages include speed and access; problems include the digital divide, information overload, cyber security and privacy.

Artificial intelligence in detail. AI refers to computer systems that perform tasks requiring human intelligence. In education, AI supports adaptive learning platforms that adjust to each learner, intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment and feedback, chatbots, translation and accessibility tools. Concerns include academic honesty, data privacy, bias, over-dependence and the need for teachers to guide responsible use.
section-9: Meaning and scope: Educational technology is the systematic application of scientific knowledge about learning and communication to improve teaching and learning. It covers objectives, learner analysis, content, media, methods and evaluation. It is a process, not merely a set of machines.

Need and importance: It helps meet the challenges of large classes, knowledge explosion, individual differences and the demand for quality. It makes learning interesting, concrete, individualised and accessible, supports distance education and improves teacher efficiency.

Types: Teaching technology focuses on the teaching process and its phases; instructional technology focuses on designing instructional materials; behavioural technology focuses on modifying teacher and learner behaviour through techniques like micro-teaching and interaction analysis.

Approaches: The hardware approach uses machines and media such as projectors, radio, television and computers. The software approach uses psychological principles to develop materials and methods. The systems approach integrates both into a planned whole with inputs, processes and outputs and continuous feedback. Effective educational technology combines all approaches to suit the learner and context.
section-10: Meaning and process: Communication is the sharing of ideas, information and feelings between a sender and a receiver through a medium, with feedback. In teaching, the teacher is the main sender, the content is the message, teaching aids and speech are channels and students are receivers. Berlo's SMCR model explains these elements.

Forms: Verbal communication uses spoken and written words; non-verbal communication uses facial expressions, gestures, posture, eye contact, voice and space. Effective teachers combine both and ensure that verbal and non-verbal messages agree.

Factors and barriers: Communication depends on the sender's clarity and attitude, the organisation of the message, suitability of the channel, the receiver's attention and readiness, and the environment. Barriers may be physical (noise), psychological (fear, disinterest), semantic (difficult words), cultural and organisational.

Improving classroom communication: Teachers should use simple language, examples and teaching aids, encourage questions, provide feedback, maintain eye contact, arrange suitable seating and create a friendly climate. Good communication is the foundation of effective teaching.
section-11: Educational objectives: Bloom's taxonomy organises objectives into cognitive, affective and psychomotor domains, each with hierarchical levels. Clear objectives guide the choice of content, methods and evaluation, and help write measurable learning outcomes.

Programmed learning: Based on Skinner's principles, programmed learning presents content in small steps with active response, immediate feedback and self-pacing. Linear, branching and mathetics programmes are its main types. It is useful for self-study and individualised instruction.

Instructional system design: ISD uses models such as ADDIE to analyse needs, design objectives and strategies, develop materials, implement instruction and evaluate it. It makes instruction systematic and improvement-oriented.

Training technology - Flanders's interaction analysis: FIACS classifies classroom verbal interaction into ten categories of teacher talk, student talk and silence. Analysis of the interaction matrix shows whether teaching is direct or indirect and helps teachers make classrooms more interactive. Micro-teaching and simulated teaching are other training techniques.
section-12: Personalized System of Instruction: Keller's PSI uses self-paced units, mastery requirements, proctors and written materials. It allows each learner to progress at their own speed and ensures mastery before moving forward.

Computer Assisted Instruction: CAI provides drill, tutorials, simulations and games with instant feedback and multimedia. It supports individualised learning but needs infrastructure and teacher support.

Informatics: The use of information and communication technology to collect, store, process and share information has transformed education through digital libraries, online courses, learning management systems and data-based planning. It improves access and speed but raises issues of the digital divide, information overload and privacy.

Artificial intelligence: AI-based adaptive platforms, intelligent tutors, automated feedback and assistive tools can personalise learning and reduce teachers' routine work. However, ethical use, data protection, avoidance of bias, academic integrity and the irreplaceable role of human teachers must be kept in mind. These innovations should be used to support, not replace, meaningful teaching.
section-15: Teaching and learning in detail. Teaching is an interactive, purposeful activity that brings desirable changes in learners; it is both an art and a science. H.C. Morrison described teaching as an intimate contact between a more mature personality and a less mature one. Learning is the outcome of teaching, but it can also happen without formal teaching. Teaching is effective only when learning takes place.

Factors affecting teaching in detail. Teacher factors (knowledge, skills, personality, attitude, health), learner factors (intelligence, motivation, readiness, background), content factors (difficulty, organisation), method and media, and environmental factors (class size, infrastructure, school climate, home support).

Levels of teaching in detail. Memory level (Herbart) - recall of facts through drill and repetition; understanding level (Morrison) - grasp of relationships, principles and meaning; reflective level (Hunt) - problem-centred, critical and creative thinking. Teaching should gradually move learners from memory to reflective level.

Principles and maxims in detail. Principles include motivation, activity, interest, linking with life, definite aim, individual differences, selection and planning. Maxims include proceeding from known to unknown, simple to complex, concrete to abstract, particular to general, whole to part, analysis to synthesis, empirical to rational, and psychological to logical.
section-16: Audio-visual aids in detail. Teaching aids appeal to the senses and make learning concrete. Edgar Dale's 'Cone of Experience' arranges experiences from the most concrete (direct purposeful experiences) to the most abstract (verbal symbols), showing that people learn more from concrete experiences.

Selection in detail. Criteria include relevance to objectives and content, suitability to the age and level of learners, accuracy and up-to-date information, simplicity and clarity, size and visibility, availability and cost, durability, and the teacher's ability to use it. Aids should be tested before use.

Types in detail. Audio aids: radio, tape recorder, audio CDs, podcasts. Visual aids: chalkboard, charts, maps, pictures, flash cards, models, specimens, flannel board, bulletin board, OHP, slides. Audio-visual aids: television, films, video, computer multimedia, smart boards, internet videos. Activity aids include field trips, dramatisation and experiments.

Advantages and disadvantages in detail. Advantages: attract attention, arouse interest, make abstract ideas concrete, save time, aid retention, help slow learners and promote active learning. Disadvantages: cost, need for electricity and equipment, time for preparation, risk of distraction if overused, and teachers' lack of training.
section-17: Lesson plan in detail. A lesson plan is the teacher's blueprint for a lesson. Herbartian steps are preparation (introduction), presentation, comparison and association, generalisation, application and recapitulation. Other approaches include Bloom's evaluation approach and the 5E constructivist model (engage, explore, explain, elaborate, evaluate). Advantages: clarity of objectives, proper sequencing, time management and confidence.

Micro-teaching in detail. Developed at Stanford University in 1963 by Dwight Allen and colleagues, micro-teaching scales down teaching: 5-10 students, 5-10 minutes and one skill at a time. The cycle is plan - teach - feedback - re-plan - re-teach - re-feedback (about 36 minutes in the Indian model). It helps student teachers master specific skills.

Teaching skills in detail. Important skills include introducing a lesson, questioning (fluency and probing questions), explaining, illustrating with examples, stimulus variation (gestures, movement, change of interaction), reinforcement (verbal and non-verbal praise), using the blackboard, achieving closure and classroom management.

Problem solving and storytelling in detail. The problem-solving method (Dewey's steps: sensing the problem, defining it, collecting data, forming hypotheses, testing and drawing conclusions) develops reasoning and scientific attitude. Storytelling makes lessons interesting, develops imagination, language and values, and is especially useful for young learners and for teaching history and moral education.
section-18: Effective teacher in detail. Qualities include mastery of subject, professional training, good communication, love for children, patience, fairness, enthusiasm, punctuality, creativity, sense of humour, emotional stability, good character and commitment to lifelong learning. Effective teachers adapt methods to learners and build positive relationships.

Planner and facilitator in detail. As a planner the teacher sets objectives, prepares lesson plans, selects methods and aids and plans co-curricular activities. As a facilitator, according to constructivism and NEP 2020, the teacher creates opportunities for exploration, discussion and discovery rather than only transmitting information.

Counsellor and evaluator in detail. As a counsellor the teacher helps students with academic, personal and career problems, identifies those who need special help and refers them to professional counsellors. As an evaluator the teacher uses continuous and comprehensive evaluation, formative assessment, tests, observation and portfolios, and provides constructive feedback.

Professional ethics in detail. Ethics include commitment to students' welfare, equal treatment without discrimination, honesty, confidentiality, respect for colleagues and parents, avoiding private tuition for one's own students, avoiding corporal punishment, continuous professional development and loyalty to the profession. NCTE and other bodies have issued codes of professional ethics for teachers.
section-20: Teaching and learning: Teaching is a purposeful, interactive process aimed at bringing desirable changes in learners; learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour through experience. Teaching is successful only when it leads to learning.

Factors affecting teaching: The teacher's competence and personality, the learner's abilities and motivation, the nature of content, methods and aids, and the classroom and school environment all influence teaching effectiveness.

Levels of teaching: Memory level (Herbart) focuses on recall; understanding level (Morrison) focuses on meaning and relationships; reflective level (Hunt) focuses on problem-solving and critical thinking. Good teaching progresses from memory to reflective level.

Principles and maxims: General principles include motivation, activity, interest, linking with life and individual differences; psychological principles include readiness, reinforcement and recreation. Maxims such as known to unknown, simple to complex, concrete to abstract and whole to part help teachers organise lessons effectively.
section-21: Meaning: Audio-visual aids are devices and materials that use hearing, sight or both to make teaching concrete, clear and interesting. Edgar Dale's Cone of Experience shows that concrete experiences are more effective than abstract verbal experiences.
Selection: Aids must suit objectives, content and learners' level; they should be accurate, clear, visible, affordable, available and within the teacher's skill.

Types: Audio aids (radio, recordings, podcasts), visual aids (chalkboard, charts, maps, models, flash cards, slides, projectors) and audio-visual aids (television, films, videos, computers, smart boards). Low-cost locally made aids are also valuable.

Advantages and limitations: Aids increase attention, interest, understanding and retention, and help different types of learners. However, they can be costly, require equipment and preparation, and may distract if overused. Teachers need training to use them properly and integrate them into lessons.
section-22: Lesson planning: A lesson plan states objectives, content, teaching-learning activities, aids, evaluation and homework. Herbartian steps and constructivist models such as 5E guide planning. Planning brings clarity, sequence and confidence.

Micro-teaching: A scaled-down teaching technique (few students, short time, one skill) with a cycle of plan, teach, feedback, re-plan, re-teach and re-feedback. It helps student teachers develop specific skills systematically.

Teaching skills: Introducing, questioning, explaining, illustrating with examples, stimulus variation, reinforcement, blackboard writing and closure are core skills that are later integrated in real teaching.

Methods - problem solving and storytelling: The problem-solving method follows the steps of scientific thinking and develops reasoning and independence. Storytelling captures interest, develops imagination, language and values, and makes abstract ideas concrete. A good teacher uses a variety of methods suited to the content and learners.
section-23: Effective teacher: An effective teacher combines subject knowledge, pedagogical skill, communication, fairness, patience, enthusiasm and genuine concern for students, and continues to learn throughout their career.

Planner and facilitator: The teacher plans lessons, activities and evaluation and acts as a facilitator who creates opportunities for students to explore, discuss and construct knowledge, as emphasised by NCF 2005 and NEP 2020.
Counsellor and evaluator: The teacher guides students in academic, personal and career matters and uses continuous and comprehensive evaluation to diagnose difficulties and support improvement.

Professional ethics: Teachers must act with integrity, treat all students fairly, respect confidentiality, avoid corporal punishment and exploitation, cooperate with colleagues and parents, and commit to professional growth. Other roles include being a role model, leader, researcher and community worker.
section-26: Special education in detail. Special education is specially designed instruction, at no cost to parents, to meet the unique needs of children with disabilities or exceptional abilities. It includes adapted curriculum, special methods, assistive devices, therapy services and trained special educators. It may be provided in special schools, integrated settings or inclusive classrooms.

Need and importance in detail. Every child has the right to education (RTE Act 2009, RPWD Act 2016). Special education helps exceptional children develop their potential, become independent, participate in society and avoid discrimination. It also helps early identification and intervention, which reduces the impact of disabilities.

Exceptional children in detail. Exceptional children deviate from the average in physical, mental, emotional or social characteristics to such an extent that they need special educational services. They include the gifted and talented, children with intellectual disability, learning disabilities, visual and hearing impairment, physical disabilities, speech and language disorders, autism, emotional and behavioural disorders and multiple disabilities.

Inclusive orientation in detail. Inclusive education means that children with and without disabilities learn together in regular schools with appropriate support. The Salamanca Statement (1994), the RPWD Act 2016, Samagra Shiksha and NEP 2020 support inclusion. Requirements include accessible buildings, trained teachers, resource rooms, assistive devices, curriculum adaptation and positive attitudes.
section-27: Visual impairment in detail. It includes blindness and low vision. Signs include rubbing eyes, holding books very close, squinting and difficulty seeing the blackboard. Educational provisions: Braille (developed by Louis Braille), large-print books, magnifiers, audio books, screen readers, tactile maps and models, orientation and mobility training, seating near the board and verbal description of visual material.

Hearing impairment in detail. It ranges from mild hearing loss to profound deafness. Signs include not responding to sounds, asking for repetition, speech problems and turning one ear toward the speaker. Provisions: hearing aids and cochlear implants, sign language (Indian Sign Language), lip-reading, total communication, visual aids, captions, seating near the teacher and speech therapy.

Physical disability in detail. Includes locomotor disabilities, cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, spinal injuries and loss of limbs. Provisions: ramps, accessible toilets and classrooms, wheelchairs, crutches, adapted furniture and writing tools, physiotherapy and occupational therapy, and adapted physical education.

Educational support in detail. Support includes early identification, Individualized Education Programmes (IEPs), resource rooms and resource teachers, assistive technology, scholarships, escort and transport allowances, curriculum adaptation, extra time in examinations, and sensitisation of peers, teachers and parents.
section-28: Intellectual disability in detail. According to AAIDD, it is characterised by significant limitations in intellectual functioning (IQ below about 70) and adaptive behaviour (conceptual, social and practical skills), originating before age 18 (now 22). Levels: mild, moderate, severe and profound. Education should focus on functional skills, daily living, simple academic skills, vocational training, task analysis, repetition and reinforcement.

Learning disability in detail. Specific learning disabilities include dyslexia (reading), dysgraphia (writing), dyscalculia (mathematics) and dyspraxia (motor coordination). Children have average or above-average intelligence but face difficulty in specific academic areas due to neurological differences, not due to poor teaching or lack of effort.

Identification in detail. Methods include teacher observation, checklists, screening tests, school records, diagnostic and achievement tests, intelligence tests, medical examinations and assessment by psychologists. Early identification is essential; tools like the NIMHANS battery are used in India.

Remedial support in detail. Remedial teaching includes multisensory methods (seeing, hearing, touching - VAKT), phonics-based reading programmes, use of concrete materials for mathematics, breaking tasks into small steps, extra time, use of technology (text-to-speech, calculators), individualised plans, positive reinforcement and cooperation between teachers, parents and specialists.
section-29: Gifted children in detail. Terman defined gifted children as those with IQ above 140, while modern definitions include creativity, leadership, artistic and other talents. Renzulli's three-ring model describes giftedness as the interaction of above-average ability, creativity and task commitment. Gardner's multiple intelligences broaden the concept.

Characteristics in detail. Intellectual: rapid learning, excellent memory, advanced vocabulary, abstract reasoning, curiosity and wide interests. Personal and social: independence, perfectionism, sensitivity, sense of humour, leadership and sometimes boredom or impatience with routine work. Some gifted children may underachieve or have behavioural problems if not challenged.

Educational needs in detail. They need challenging and complex tasks, freedom to explore, opportunities for creative and critical thinking, understanding teachers, guidance for emotional and social adjustment, and recognition without excessive pressure.

Educational provisions in detail. Enrichment (broader and deeper content, projects, clubs, competitions), acceleration (early admission, grade skipping, advanced courses), ability grouping, mentoring, independent study, special schools and programmes such as the National Talent Search Examination, KVPY (earlier), INSPIRE scholarships and Olympiads.
section-31: Meaning: Special education is specially designed instruction and support to meet the unique needs of exceptional children through adapted curriculum, methods, materials, assistive devices and trained teachers.

Need and importance: It ensures the right to education for all, helps exceptional children reach their potential and become independent, enables early intervention and reduces discrimination. Laws such as the RTE Act 2009 and the RPWD Act 2016 make it a legal obligation.

Exceptional children: They include the gifted and talented, and children with intellectual disability, learning disabilities, sensory impairments, physical disabilities, speech and language disorders, autism, emotional and behavioural disorders and multiple disabilities.

From segregation to inclusion: Education of children with disabilities has moved from special schools (segregation) to integrated education (IEDC, 1974) and inclusive education. The Salamanca Statement (1994), UNCRPD (2006), RPWD Act 2016, Samagra Shiksha and NEP 2020 emphasise inclusive schools with accessibility, trained teachers, resource support and positive attitudes.
section-32: Visual impairment: Children who are blind or have low vision need Braille, large print, magnifiers, audio materials, screen readers, tactile materials and orientation and mobility training. Teachers should describe visual material verbally and seat them appropriately.

Hearing impairment: Children with hearing loss need early identification, hearing aids or cochlear implants, sign language or total communication, speech therapy, visual aids and captions. Teachers should face the class while speaking and use written instructions.

Physical disability: Children with locomotor disabilities or cerebral palsy need barrier-free buildings, ramps, accessible toilets, wheelchairs, adapted furniture and writing tools, physiotherapy and adapted physical education.

Educational support: IEPs, resource rooms, assistive technology, examination accommodations (extra time, scribes), scholarships and transport allowances under Samagra Shiksha, and sensitisation of peers and teachers help these children participate fully in school life.
section-33: Intellectual disability: Characterised by limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour before adulthood. Education focuses on functional academics, daily living skills, social skills and vocational training using task analysis, repetition, concrete materials and positive reinforcement.

Learning disability: Specific learning disabilities like dyslexia, dysgraphia and dyscalculia affect particular academic skills despite normal intelligence. They are lifelong but can be managed with suitable support.
Identification: Observation, checklists, screening and diagnostic tests, intelligence and achievement tests, school records and professional assessment help identify these children early.

Remedial support: Multisensory teaching, phonics, concrete materials, small steps, assistive technology, extra time, individualised plans, remedial classes and cooperation with parents and specialists help children overcome difficulties and build confidence.
section-34: Concept of giftedness: Gifted children show exceptionally high ability or potential in intellectual, creative, artistic, leadership or academic areas. Renzulli's model combines above-average ability, creativity and task commitment.

Characteristics: They learn quickly, have advanced vocabulary and reasoning, are curious, creative and independent, and often show perfectionism and sensitivity. They may become bored or underachieve in an unchallenging environment.
Educational needs: They need challenging work, opportunities for creativity and research, guidance for social and emotional adjustment and recognition of their talents.

Provisions: Enrichment programmes, acceleration, ability grouping, mentoring, independent projects, special schools and national programmes such as NTSE, INSPIRE and Olympiads. Teachers should identify gifted students through observation, tests and achievement and provide differentiated instruction.
section-38: Meaning and structure in detail. Higher education begins after Class XII and includes undergraduate, postgraduate, M.Phil (discontinued under NEP 2020), Ph.D., diploma and professional programmes. India has one of the largest higher education systems in the world, with over 1,000 universities and around 40,000 colleges. Institutions include universities, affiliated colleges, autonomous colleges and institutes of national importance (IITs, IIMs, AIIMS, NITs).

Objectives and goals in detail. According to the Radhakrishnan Commission and NEP 2020, higher education aims at advancement of knowledge through teaching and research, development of the whole person, preparation of leaders and professionals, promotion of democratic values, social justice and national integration, innovation and economic development.

Types of universities in detail. Central universities (established by Acts of Parliament, e.g. Mizoram University, 2001), state universities (established by state legislatures), private universities, deemed-to-be universities (declared by the central government under Section 3 of the UGC Act) and institutes of national importance. Open universities like IGNOU provide distance education.

Constitutional provisions in detail. Education is in the Concurrent List (after the 42nd Amendment, 1976). Entry 66 of the Union List gives Parliament the power of coordination and determination of standards in higher education. Articles 15(4), 15(5) and 46 provide for reservations and educational advancement of weaker sections; Articles 29 and 30 protect minority institutions.
section-39: Internationalisation in detail. It includes student and faculty exchange, joint and dual degree programmes, international research collaboration, campuses of foreign universities in India (permitted under NEP 2020 and UGC regulations of 2023), Indian institutions setting up campuses abroad and attracting foreign students through the 'Study in India' programme.

Autonomy in detail. Autonomous colleges have freedom to design curricula, methods of teaching and evaluation and to conduct examinations, while degrees are awarded by the parent university. Autonomy promotes innovation and quality but requires accountability through accreditation. NEP 2020 plans to phase out the affiliation system and make colleges autonomous degree-granting institutions.

NEP 2020 innovations in detail. Multidisciplinary education, flexible four-year undergraduate programme with multiple entry and exit, Academic Bank of Credits, choice of subjects across streams, National Research Foundation, Common University Entrance Test, online and digital education, vocational education integration and the Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) as a single regulator.

LPG in detail. Liberalisation reduced state control and allowed private institutions; privatisation increased the number of private universities and self-financing courses; globalisation increased competition, international standards and mobility. Benefits include expansion and choice; concerns include commercialisation, high fees, uneven quality and reduced access for the poor.
section-40: UGC in detail. The University Grants Commission was established in 1953 and became a statutory body through the UGC Act 1956. It coordinates and maintains standards of university education, allocates grants to universities and colleges, frames regulations (such as minimum qualifications for teachers), conducts UGC-NET (now through NTA) and recognises universities. NEP 2020 proposes replacing it with HECI.

NAAC in detail. The National Assessment and Accreditation Council was established in 1994 by the UGC and is headquartered in Bengaluru. It assesses institutions on criteria such as curricular aspects, teaching-learning and evaluation, research and innovation, infrastructure, student support, governance and institutional values. Grades range from A++ to C, based on a cumulative grade point average. Accreditation encourages quality improvement.

RUSA in detail. Rashtriya Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan was launched in 2013 as a centrally sponsored scheme to improve access, equity and quality in state higher education institutions. It provides funds for new universities and colleges, infrastructure, faculty improvement, research and governance reforms, based on state higher education plans.

Higher education in NEP 2020 in detail. Targets include a GER of 50 per cent by 2035, holistic multidisciplinary education, large multidisciplinary universities and clusters, phasing out affiliation, light but tight regulation, research promotion through NRF, quality teacher education (four-year integrated B.Ed.), and internationalisation.
section-41: Access and equity in detail. India's GER in higher education is around 28 per cent (AISHE 2021-22), lower than in developed countries. Disparities exist by region, gender, caste, tribe, income and disability. Rural and hilly areas like the North-East have fewer institutions. Measures include scholarships, reservations, new institutions, distance and online education and hostels.

Quality and excellence in detail. Problems include shortage of qualified faculty, outdated curricula, rote learning, inadequate research, poor infrastructure and low global rankings. Measures include accreditation (NAAC, NBA), the National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF), faculty development, research funding and Institutions of Eminence.

Growing unemployment in detail. Many graduates lack employable skills due to mismatch between education and job market needs. Solutions include skill-based courses, internships, apprenticeships, vocational education, entrepreneurship development, industry linkages and career guidance.

Resource crunch in detail. Public spending on education is below the recommended 6 per cent of GDP. Institutions face shortages of funds for infrastructure, research and faculty. Solutions include increased public funding, the Higher Education Financing Agency (HEFA), alumni and industry contributions, efficient use of resources and research grants.
section-43: Meaning and structure: Higher education covers education after the higher secondary stage, including undergraduate, postgraduate, research and professional courses offered by universities, colleges and specialised institutions.

Objectives: It aims at advancing knowledge through teaching and research, developing individuals holistically, training professionals and leaders, promoting democratic values and social justice and contributing to national development.

Types of universities: Central, state, private and deemed universities, institutes of national importance and open universities form India's higher education structure. Mizoram University is a central university established in 2001.

Constitutional provisions: Education is a Concurrent List subject; Entry 66 of the Union List empowers Parliament to coordinate and maintain standards; Articles 15(4), 15(5), 46, 29 and 30 promote equity and protect minority institutions. Bodies like UGC, AICTE and NCTE regulate different sectors of higher education.
section-44: Internationalisation: Student and faculty exchange, joint programmes, research collaboration and foreign campuses improve quality and global exposure. NEP 2020 and UGC regulations encourage this.

Autonomy: Academic and administrative autonomy allows institutions to innovate in curricula and evaluation while remaining accountable through accreditation. NEP 2020 aims to make colleges autonomous degree-granting institutions.

NEP 2020 innovations: Multidisciplinary universities, flexible four-year undergraduate programmes with multiple entry and exit, Academic Bank of Credits, National Research Foundation, CUET and a single regulator (HECI) are major reforms.

LPG and higher education: Liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation expanded private institutions, self-financing courses and international competition. They increased access and choice but also raised concerns about commercialisation, high fees and unequal quality. Balanced regulation is needed to ensure equity and quality.
section-45: UGC: As the statutory body for higher education (1956), the UGC coordinates standards, provides grants, frames regulations and recognises universities.

NAAC: Established in 1994, NAAC assesses and accredits institutions on criteria such as curriculum, teaching-learning, research, infrastructure, student support, governance and best practices, encouraging continuous quality improvement.
RUSA: Launched in 2013, RUSA funds state higher education institutions to improve access, equity and quality through planning, infrastructure, faculty development and governance reforms.

NEP 2020: It aims at a 50 per cent GER by 2035, multidisciplinary education, research promotion, phasing out affiliation, autonomy, technology use and a single regulator (HECI) with separate verticals for regulation, accreditation, funding and standard-setting. Together these bodies plan and manage higher education for quality and equity.
section-46: Access and equity: Low GER and disparities based on region, gender, caste, income and disability limit participation. Scholarships, reservation, new institutions, hostels and online education help widen access.

Quality and excellence: Shortage of faculty, outdated curricula, poor research culture and infrastructure lower quality. Accreditation, NIRF rankings, faculty development and research funding are remedies.

Growing unemployment: A mismatch between degrees and market needs causes graduate unemployment. Skill-based programmes, internships, industry collaboration, vocational education and entrepreneurship can improve employability.

Resource crunch: Inadequate funding limits infrastructure, research and faculty recruitment. Increasing public investment toward 6 per cent of GDP, HEFA loans, industry and alumni contributions and efficient management are needed. Other problems include politicisation, examination malpractice and brain drain.
section-49: Educational planning in detail. Coombs defined educational planning as the application of rational, systematic analysis to the process of educational development with the aim of making education more effective and efficient in responding to the needs and goals of students and society. In India, educational planning was part of the Five-Year Plans and is now guided by policies like NEP 2020 and schemes like Samagra Shiksha.

Need and importance in detail. Resources are limited while educational needs are vast. Planning helps fix priorities, avoid wastage, coordinate different levels and agencies, link education with manpower needs, ensure equity and quality, and evaluate progress.

Principles in detail. Planning should be goal-oriented, realistic and feasible, comprehensive, flexible, participatory (involving teachers, community and administrators), based on reliable data, integrated with national development plans, and continuously evaluated.

Types in detail. By level: national, state, district (decentralised), institutional and micro-level planning. By duration: long-term (perspective, 15-20 years), medium-term (5 years) and short-term (annual). By purpose: academic planning, financial planning, physical (infrastructure) planning and manpower planning.
section-50: Planning process in detail. Steps: (1) diagnosis of the present situation using data; (2) assessment of needs and demands; (3) formulation of goals and objectives; (4) identification of alternative strategies; (5) cost estimation and resource allocation; (6) preparation of the plan; (7) implementation; (8) monitoring and evaluation; (9) feedback and revision.

Social demand approach in detail. It plans education according to the number of students who want education at different levels, based on population growth, enrolment trends and people's aspirations. Merits: democratic and politically acceptable. Limitations: may cause educated unemployment and ignore economic needs and resource limits.

Manpower requirement approach in detail. It plans education according to the projected needs of the economy for different categories of skilled workers (engineers, doctors, teachers). Merits: links education with employment. Limitations: difficulty in forecasting manpower needs accurately, ignores social demand and individual choice.

Cost-benefit (rate of return) approach in detail. It compares the costs of education (direct costs and earnings foregone) with the benefits (higher lifetime earnings and social benefits). Investment is made in levels and types of education with the highest rate of return. Limitations: difficulty in measuring non-economic benefits and future earnings.
section-51: Educational management in detail. It is the process of planning, organising, directing and controlling human, material and financial resources to achieve educational goals efficiently. It applies management principles (Fayol, Taylor, Gulick's POSDCORB) to education at the national, state, district and institutional levels.

Functions in detail. POSDCORB - Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting and Budgeting. Other functions include supervision, evaluation and communication. These functions ensure that educational activities proceed smoothly toward goals.

Leadership in detail. Leadership styles include autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire (Lewin); transformational leadership inspires change and vision; instructional leadership focuses on improving teaching and learning. A good educational leader has vision, communication, decision-making ability, integrity and the ability to motivate staff and students.

Decision making in detail. Steps: identifying the problem, collecting information, developing alternatives, evaluating alternatives, choosing the best option, implementing and evaluating the decision. Participative decision-making involving teachers, students and parents leads to better acceptance and results.
section-52: Institutional management in detail. It includes academic management (curriculum, timetable, teaching, examinations), staff management (recruitment, duties, professional development), student management (admission, discipline, welfare, co-curricular activities), record management (admission register, attendance, cumulative records, stock register), financial management (budget, fees, accounts, audit) and physical resource management (buildings, laboratories, library).

Head of institution in detail. The principal or headmaster is the leader, administrator, academic guide, supervisor, coordinator and public relations officer of the institution. Responsibilities include planning, maintaining discipline, supervising teaching, managing finances, ensuring school-community relations and promoting innovation.

Supervision in detail. Modern supervision is democratic, cooperative and creative, aimed at improving teaching and learning rather than fault-finding inspection. Methods include classroom visits, demonstration lessons, workshops, conferences, feedback and peer observation.

Quality management in detail. Total Quality Management (TQM) in education emphasises continuous improvement, involvement of all stakeholders, focus on learners' needs, data-based decisions and teamwork. Tools include quality circles, internal quality assurance cells (IQAC), accreditation, school self-evaluation (Shaala Siddhi) and feedback systems.
section-54: Meaning: Educational planning is a rational, systematic process of deciding future educational goals and the means to achieve them, using limited resources effectively.

Need and importance: It helps set priorities, avoid wastage, coordinate efforts at different levels, meet manpower needs, promote equity and quality, and evaluate progress. India's Five-Year Plans and current schemes show the importance of planning in education.
Principles: Planning must be goal-oriented, realistic, comprehensive, flexible, participatory, data-based, integrated with national development and subject to evaluation.

Types: Planning can be national, state, district (decentralised), institutional or micro-level; long-term, medium-term or short-term; and academic, financial, physical or manpower-oriented. Decentralised and institutional planning involve local communities and teachers, making plans more relevant.
section-55: Planning process: Diagnosis, needs assessment, goal setting, choosing strategies, costing and resource allocation, plan formulation, implementation, monitoring, evaluation and revision form a continuous cycle.
Social demand approach: Education is provided according to people's demand. It is democratic but may lead to over-expansion and educated unemployment.

Manpower requirement approach: Education is planned according to the projected needs of the economy for skilled workers. It links education with jobs, but forecasting is difficult and individual choice is ignored.

Cost-benefit approach: Educational investment is guided by comparison of costs and returns. It promotes efficiency but cannot fully measure social and non-economic benefits. In practice planners combine the three approaches to balance social, economic and efficiency goals.
section-56: Meaning: Educational management is the coordination of human, material and financial resources through planning, organising, directing and controlling to achieve educational objectives effectively.
Functions: Gulick's POSDCORB (planning, organising, staffing, directing, coordinating, reporting and budgeting), along with supervision and evaluation, describe the main managerial functions.

Leadership: Educational leaders may be autocratic, democratic or laissez-faire; transformational and instructional leadership are particularly effective for improving schools. Good leaders inspire, communicate, motivate and build teamwork.

Decision making: A systematic decision-making process - defining the problem, collecting data, generating and evaluating alternatives, choosing, implementing and reviewing - leads to better outcomes. Participative decision-making increases commitment of staff and stakeholders.
section-57: Institutional management: Managing academics, staff, students, records, finance and physical resources ensures smooth functioning of schools and colleges.
Head of institution: The head is the leader, administrator, supervisor and coordinator responsible for planning, discipline, academic quality, finances and community relations.
Supervision: Modern supervision is democratic and supportive, using classroom observation, workshops, demonstration lessons and feedback to improve teaching.

Quality management: TQM, IQACs, accreditation, school self-evaluation and stakeholder feedback promote continuous improvement. Effective institutional management creates a positive climate where teachers teach well and students learn well.
section-60: Mental health in detail. The WHO describes mental health as a state of well-being in which a person realises their abilities, copes with normal stresses, works productively and contributes to the community. It is not merely the absence of mental illness; it includes emotional balance, realistic self-concept and good social relations.

Mental hygiene in detail. The mental hygiene movement was started by Clifford Beers ('A Mind That Found Itself', 1908). Mental hygiene includes preventive measures (healthy environment, guidance), preservative measures (maintaining good mental health) and curative measures (early treatment).

Objectives in detail. Preservation of mental health, prevention of mental disorders, early identification and treatment, development of integrated personality, healthy adjustment in home, school and society, and public awareness to reduce stigma.

Determinants in detail. Biological factors (heredity, health, nervous system), family factors (child rearing, parental relations, broken homes), school factors (teacher behaviour, curriculum load, examinations), social factors (poverty, discrimination, peer pressure, media) and psychological factors (stress, frustration, conflict, self-esteem).
section-61: Wholesome personality in detail. It is an integrated personality with realistic self-understanding, emotional maturity, social adjustment, sense of responsibility, a clear philosophy of life and consistent behaviour. It develops through supportive home and school environments.

Abnormal personality in detail. Abnormality is judged by deviation from statistical norms, violation of social norms, personal distress and maladaptive behaviour. Causes can be biological, psychological and social. Examples include anxiety, depression, phobias and personality disorders.

Mentally healthy person in detail. According to Marie Jahoda, criteria include positive attitude toward self, growth and self-actualisation, integration, autonomy, accurate perception of reality and environmental mastery. Such a person copes with stress, maintains satisfying relationships and works productively.

Classification in detail. Traditionally, disorders are classified into neuroses (anxiety, phobia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, hysteria) and psychoses (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder). Modern systems are DSM-5 and ICD-11, which include categories like anxiety disorders, mood disorders, neurodevelopmental disorders, personality disorders and substance use disorders.
section-62: Play therapy in detail. Developed by Anna Freud, Melanie Klein and Virginia Axline, play therapy allows children to express feelings and conflicts through toys, dolls, sand, clay, puppets and drawing. The therapist observes and helps the child understand and resolve emotions. It is useful for trauma, anxiety and behaviour problems.

Behaviour therapy in detail. Based on Pavlov, Watson and Skinner, it treats maladaptive behaviour as learned and modifiable. Techniques include positive reinforcement, token economy, systematic desensitisation (Wolpe), modelling (Bandura), aversion therapy and shaping.

Counselling therapy in detail. Includes client-centred therapy (Rogers), cognitive-behavioural therapy (Beck), rational emotive behaviour therapy (Ellis) and group counselling. It helps individuals gain insight, change negative thinking and develop coping skills.

Remedial purpose in detail. These techniques aim to reduce emotional distress, correct maladaptive behaviour, improve adjustment and social skills, and restore healthy functioning. Teachers can use simple behavioural techniques and refer students to professionals when necessary.
section-63: Adjustment in detail. Adjustment is a continuous process by which a person changes behaviour to achieve harmony between personal needs and environmental demands. Areas include home, school, health, social and emotional adjustment.

Maladjustment in detail. Signs include aggression, withdrawal, anxiety, truancy, lying, stealing, poor academic performance and nervous habits. Causes include unhealthy home conditions, school pressure, physical problems, social factors and repeated frustration.

Adjustment mechanisms in detail. Defence mechanisms described by Freud include repression, rationalisation, projection, displacement, regression, sublimation, compensation, identification and day-dreaming. Moderate use reduces anxiety, but excessive use avoids reality. Direct coping such as problem-solving is healthier.

Mental conflict in detail. Lewin's types: approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance, approach-avoidance and double approach-avoidance. Conflicts cause tension and indecision; remedies include clear values, realistic goals, careful decision-making, guidance and counselling, and stress management.
section-65: Mental health: Mental health is a state of well-being involving emotional balance, realistic thinking, productive work and good relationships, not just the absence of illness.
Mental hygiene: It is the science and practice of preserving mental health, preventing disorders and treating them early. Its pioneer was Clifford Beers.
Objectives: To preserve mental health, prevent mental illness, cure disorders early, develop an integrated personality and promote healthy adjustment.

Determinants: Heredity and health, family environment and child rearing, school climate, peer group, socio-economic conditions and psychological factors like stress and self-esteem determine mental health. Schools can promote mental hygiene through a friendly climate, guidance services, life-skills education and early identification of problems.
section-66: Wholesome personality: An integrated personality shows self-understanding, emotional maturity, social adjustment and responsibility.
Abnormal personality: Persistent maladaptive patterns that cause distress and interfere with functioning, arising from biological, psychological and social causes.
Mentally healthy person: Jahoda's criteria - positive self-attitude, growth, integration, autonomy, accurate perception of reality and environmental mastery - describe mental health.

Classification: Neuroses and psychoses in traditional terms, and DSM-5 and ICD-11 categories in modern terms, help professionals diagnose and treat disorders. Teachers should know basic signs to identify students who need help.
section-67: Play therapy: It uses play materials to help children express and work through emotions they cannot verbalise, and is effective for young children with anxiety or trauma.
Behaviour therapy: It applies learning principles - reinforcement, desensitisation, token economy, modelling - to replace maladaptive behaviour with adaptive behaviour.
Counselling therapy: Client-centred, cognitive-behavioural and group counselling provide a supportive relationship to help individuals understand problems and develop coping strategies.

Remedial purpose and role of teachers: These techniques aim at better emotional, behavioural and social functioning. Teachers can contribute through observation, simple behaviour modification, supportive relationships and referral to counsellors and psychologists.
section-68: Adjustment: Adjustment means achieving harmony between one's needs and the demands of the environment, shown by emotional balance, social acceptance and realistic goals.
Maladjustment: Persistent difficulty in coping, shown through aggression, withdrawal, anxiety and poor performance, caused by home, school, personal and social factors.

Adjustment mechanisms: Defence mechanisms like repression, rationalisation, projection, displacement, regression, sublimation and compensation reduce anxiety but should not replace realistic problem-solving.

Mental conflict: Approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance and approach-avoidance conflicts cause tension. Guidance, counselling, clear values, realistic decision-making and stress management help resolve conflicts and promote healthy adjustment.
section-71: Life skills in detail. WHO (1997) defines life skills as abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour that enable individuals to deal effectively with the demands and challenges of everyday life. WHO identified ten core life skills: self-awareness, empathy, critical thinking, creative thinking, decision making, problem solving, effective communication, interpersonal relationships, coping with stress and coping with emotions.

Need and importance in detail. Young people face peer pressure, substance abuse, academic stress, relationship problems, career choices and digital risks. Life skills help them make healthy choices, prevent risky behaviour, improve mental health, build confidence and become responsible citizens.

Life skills education in detail. It is a participatory, experiential approach using role plays, group discussions, case studies, games, brainstorming, debates and storytelling. In India it is integrated into the Adolescence Education Programme, School Health Programme under Ayushman Bharat and NEP 2020.

Role of education in detail. Schools can provide a safe environment, train teachers as facilitators, integrate life skills into subjects and co-curricular activities, involve parents and community, and use counselling services. Teachers should model these skills themselves.
section-72: Critical thinking in detail. It involves analysing information, questioning assumptions, evaluating evidence, recognising bias and drawing logical conclusions. It helps students resist misinformation, peer pressure and advertising, and make informed choices. Teachers develop it through open-ended questions, debates, case studies and analysis of media.

Creative thinking in detail. It involves fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration (Guilford, Torrance). It helps find new solutions, adapt to change and express oneself. Activities like brainstorming, art, storytelling, projects and 'what if' questions develop it.

Decision making in detail. Steps: identify the decision, gather information, list alternatives, consider consequences (pros and cons), choose the best option, act and evaluate. Good decision-making helps in matters such as career choice, health, relationships and avoiding risky behaviour.

Problem solving in detail. Steps: identify and define the problem, find its causes, generate possible solutions, evaluate them, select and implement a solution, and review results. It reduces stress and helps individuals deal with challenges constructively.
section-73: Effective communication in detail. It includes verbal and non-verbal expression, active listening, assertiveness (expressing one's views respectfully), giving and receiving feedback and saying 'no' to undesirable pressure. Barriers include poor listening, emotions and prejudice. Role plays and group discussions develop it.

Interpersonal relationship in detail. It is the ability to form and maintain positive relationships with family, friends, teachers and others, and to end unhealthy relationships constructively. It involves trust, respect, cooperation, conflict resolution and understanding.

Empathy in detail. Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of another person, 'putting oneself in another's shoes'. It reduces prejudice and bullying, promotes kindness and helps in supporting people who are different or in difficulty.

Cooperation in detail. Cooperation means working together with others to achieve shared goals, sharing responsibilities, respecting others' contributions and resolving differences. Group projects, team games, cooperative learning and community service build this skill.
section-74: Self-awareness in detail. It is recognising one's own character, strengths, weaknesses, desires, values and emotions. It is the foundation of other life skills because it helps in setting goals, making decisions and understanding how one is influenced by others. Activities include self-reflection, journals, SWOT analysis and feedback.

Coping with emotions in detail. It involves recognising emotions in oneself and others, understanding their effects on behaviour and responding appropriately. Strategies include expressing feelings in healthy ways, anger management (counting, deep breathing, time-out), talking to trusted people and engaging in creative activities.

Coping with stress in detail. Stress arises from examinations, family problems, competition and relationships. Healthy strategies include time management, regular exercise, yoga and meditation, adequate sleep, balanced diet, hobbies, positive thinking, seeking social support and counselling. Unhealthy strategies like substance use must be avoided.

Application in detail. Life skills are applied in studies (planning, concentration), health (avoiding drugs, healthy habits), relationships (communication, empathy), career choice (decision-making), digital life (critical use of social media) and citizenship (cooperation, responsibility).
section-76: Meaning of life skills: Life skills, according to WHO, are abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour that help individuals deal effectively with everyday challenges. The ten core life skills include self-awareness, empathy, critical and creative thinking, decision making, problem solving, communication, interpersonal relationships and coping with stress and emotions.

Need and importance: Adolescents face peer pressure, academic stress, substance abuse, relationship and career issues and online risks. Life skills help them make healthy choices, prevent risky behaviour, improve mental health and become confident, responsible citizens.

Life skills education: It uses participatory and experiential methods - role plays, discussions, case studies, games and projects - rather than lectures. It is part of programmes like the Adolescence Education Programme and the School Health Programme.

Role of education: Schools and teachers should create a supportive environment, integrate life skills into the curriculum and co-curricular activities, train teachers as facilitators, involve parents and provide counselling. NEP 2020 emphasises holistic development including these skills.
section-77: Critical thinking: Analysing information, questioning assumptions and evaluating evidence helps learners avoid misinformation and make informed choices.
Creative thinking: Generating original and flexible ideas helps learners adapt to change, solve problems in new ways and express themselves.
Decision making: A systematic process of identifying choices, considering consequences and choosing the best option helps in important life decisions about studies, health and relationships.

Problem solving: Defining a problem, exploring causes and alternatives, selecting and implementing a solution and reviewing results helps individuals handle challenges constructively. These thinking skills are interrelated and can be developed through open-ended questions, debates, projects and real-life case studies.
section-78: Effective communication: Clear verbal and non-verbal expression, active listening and assertiveness help individuals express their needs and resist negative pressure.
Interpersonal relationships: The ability to build and maintain healthy relationships based on trust, respect and cooperation supports emotional well-being.
Empathy: Understanding others' feelings and perspectives promotes kindness, reduces conflict and bullying and helps people support each other.

Cooperation: Working together toward shared goals, sharing tasks and respecting others' contributions are essential in school, family, work and community. Group work, team sports and community service are effective ways to develop these social skills.
section-79: Self-awareness: Knowing one's strengths, weaknesses, values and feelings is the foundation for setting goals and making good decisions.
Coping with emotions: Recognising and managing emotions such as anger, fear and sadness in healthy ways helps maintain relationships and mental health.
Coping with stress: Time management, exercise, relaxation, hobbies, positive thinking and seeking support help manage stress from studies and life events.

Application: Personal and emotional skills help learners manage studies, relationships, health choices and everyday challenges more effectively. When combined with thinking and social skills, they help young people lead balanced, healthy and productive lives.
